_strings.@@0e275c6b0f4d: Child and Dependent Care Credit — Resident taxpayers who have earned income, paid someone to care for one or more qualifying persons so they could work or look for work, and who were allowed the federal child and dependent care credit (civil-union and non-joint-federal filers compute a mock federal credit per the Worksheet J instructions). Married filing separately is only eligible if the federal exceptions are met.
_strings.@@15e4c9a0d161: New Jersey Child Tax Credit — Resident taxpayers with NJ taxable income (line 42) of $80,000 or less, claiming a credit for each dependent who is age 5 or younger on the last day of the tax year. The dependent must be claimed on the NJ-1040 dependent lines. Married filing separately is not eligible. Part-year residents prorate by months of NJ residency.
_strings.@@1b090f3f0709: Print only the form pages (not instructions), single-sided; attach state copies of W-2/1099.
_strings.@@1bd88755f36e: New Jersey Earned Income Tax Credit (NJEITC) — New Jersey residents who work and have earned income and who claimed and were allowed the federal Earned Income Credit (EIC). Residents at least 18 years old on the last day of the tax year who meet all federal EIC requirements EXCEPT the age requirement, had no qualifying child, and are not listed as a dependent on another tax return may claim a fixed NJEITC even without a federal EIC - the maximum age limit has been eliminated. Married filing separately qualifies only with a qualifying child who lived with the filer more than half of 2025 and living apart from the spouse for the last six months of 2025. Part-year residents prorate by months of NJ residency.
_strings.@@2ad4d6c65d46: Property Tax Deduction/Credit (homeowners and tenants) — Residents who were domiciled in NJ and maintained a principal residence (main home) as a homeowner or tenant during 2025 that was subject to property taxes (paid directly as a homeowner, or through rent for tenants - 18% of rent, or 18% of mobile-home site fees, counts as property taxes paid). Taxpayer takes EITHER the deduction OR the credit (whichever gives the greater benefit; Worksheet H decides). Homeowners or tenants age 65 or older or disabled who are below the filing threshold can claim the credit on Form NJ-1040-HW without filing NJ-1040 (by April 15, 2026).

_strings.@@33291489b9ac: NJ grants a six-month extension of time to FILE if you pay at least 80% of your tax liability (line 45) through withholdings, estimated payments, or other payments by the original due date AND either enclose a copy of the federal automatic-extension application (filling in the oval on the front of the NJ-1040) or file Form NJ-630 by April 15, 2026; the extension application can be filed online until 11:59 p.m. April 15, 2026 at nj.gov/taxation. If you do not meet the requirements, or do not file by the extended due date, the Division will deny the extension request.
_strings.@@4437c6037806: If any income was exempt from federal tax under a treaty: NJ does not conform to federal tax treaties — that income is still taxable to NJ.
_strings.@@4b757408f1b2: Treaty conformity — NJ does NOT conform to federal tax treaties: income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is STILL taxable by NJ. Do not carry a federal treaty exclusion onto the state return. (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state's Internal Revenue Code conformity date and its deduction/credit conformity are separate questions; see any law-change lines below.) State note: New Jersey does NOT start from federal AGI. The NJ Gross Income Tax is a self-contained system that builds gross income from its own statutory categories. The 2025 NJ-1040 instructions explicitly direct, in "Things to Know Before You Begin" (p. 4): "Use 'State Wages' from box 16 of your W-2, not federal wages (box 1)." Because NJ never imports federal AGI, a federal tax-treaty exemption (which reduces federal box 1 / federal AGI) does NOT automatically pass through. The word "treaty" appears ZERO times in the 2025 NJ-1040 instruction booklet (re-counted this session across all 70 pages), and NJ's Gross Income Tax Act contains no provision recognizing federal income tax treaties, so federally treaty-exempt wages are generally still taxable for NJ purposes. This puts NJ in the "builds income from scratch, no treaty pass-through" category -> conforms_to_federal_treaties = false. (Conservative reading; the precise NJ treatment of a specific treaty article should be confirmed at the DOR.)

This op computes the state's rate-schedule tax line ONLY — county/city add-on taxes, state credits, and any amounts outside the rate schedule are NOT modeled. Pack notes: Base guidance: Supply Form NJ-1040 Line 29, New Jersey Gross Income (Line 27 total income minus the Line 28c pension/retirement exclusion). NJ never starts from federal AGI — gross income is built from NJ's own categories (wages from W-2 box 16 'State wages,' not federal box 1, per 'Things to Know Before You Begin,' 2025 booklet p. 4). The op subtracts $1,000 x exemptions_count (Line 6 regular exemptions: self, spouse/CU partner, or registered domestic partner) and $1,500 x dependents_count (Line 10 qualified dependent children plus Line 11 other dependents) to approximate Line 42 New Jersey Taxable Income. If any UNMODELED subtraction applies — Line 7 senior 65+ ($1,000 each), Line 8 blind/disabled ($1,000 each), Line 9 veteran ($6,000 each), Line 12 dependent attending college ($1,000 each), Lines 31-37c deductions (medical over 2% of gross income, alimony, qualified conservation contribution, health enterprise zone, alternative business calculation adjustment, organ/bone marrow donation up to $10,000, NJBEST up to $10,000, NJCLASS up to $2,500, tuition up to $10,000), or the Line 41 Property Tax Deduction (up to $15,000; $7,500 if you and your spouse file separately but maintained the same main home) — reduce the supplied base by those amounts too, or compute on the form; otherwise the result will overstate Line 43. Adjudication note (two-pass, TY2025): the 2025 Tables A and B were drafted from the resident booklet (p. 63) and re-verified against the 2025 NJ-1040NR instructions (p. 44) — identical schedules, and NJ's brackets are STATUTORY and UNCHANGED (same seven/eight-bracket schedules in force since the 2020 millionaire's-tax addition; the 2025 print matches the 2024 and 2023 prints digit for digit, including every STEP 3 subtraction constant). All printed STEP 3 constants were re-reconciled against exact cumulative bracket math for 2025: every constant is exact EXCEPT Table B's -$1,154.50 (see the misprint note below). Tax Table MANDATE below $100,000: Line 43 directs 'If the income on line 42 is less than $100,000, use the Tax Table on page 54. Otherwise, calculate the tax by using the Tax Rate Schedules on page 63.' The 2025 Tax Table header repeats it: 'Use this table if your New Jersey taxable income on line 42 is less than $100,000. If your taxable income is $100,000 or more, you must use the Tax Rate Schedules on page 63.' Bracket math may differ by a few dollars within a $50 table band (the table is banded in $50 steps, e.g. the booklet's own example: taxable income $39,875 -> $628 for filing status 2); the filed form MUST use the table below $100,000. The Tax Rate Schedules (shipped here) govern at $100,000 and above. Filing threshold = no tax due: you are not required to file (and owe no NJ tax) if New Jersey gross income (Line 29) is at or below $10,000 (single; married/CU partner filing separate) or $20,000 (married/CU couple filing joint; head of household; qualifying widow(er)/surviving CU partner). NOT modeled — the brackets tax from the first dollar, so below-threshold filers would be overstated; file only to recover withholding or refundable credits. CRITICAL — printed-constant divergence (Table B only), the famous misprint constant PERSISTS FOR 2025: the $70,000-$80,000 bracket prints 'multiply by .035, subtract $1,154.50', but the exact cumulative constant is $1,155.00 (20,000 x .014 = 280.00, plus 30,000 x .0175 = 525.00, plus 20,000 x .0245 = 490.00 = 1,295.00 at $70,000, and .035 x 70,000 = 2,450.00, so the exact subtraction is 2,450.00 - 1,295.00 = 1,155.00). The printed schedule therefore yields $0.50 MORE than exact marginal-bracket math everywhere inside that bracket, and rejoins exactly at $80,000 (the next constant, $2,775.00, is exact). Because NJ rounds to whole dollars, that $0.50 can become a $1 difference: at taxable income $70,200 exact math gives $1,302.00 -> $1,302 while the printed schedule gives $1,302.50 -> $1,303. Every other printed constant in Tables A and B equals the cumulative sum exactly. The same $1,154.50 appears in both the 2025 resident (p. 63) and nonresident (p. 44) prints, as it has since 2020 — it is a durable print, not a one-year typo. One schedule covers three statuses: Table B applies identically to married/CU couple filing joint return, head of household, and qualifying widow(er)/surviving CU partner — the head_of_household brackets shipped here are Table B, identical to married_filing_jointly, and the engine's QSS->married_filing_jointly mapping is exact (no divergence). Table A applies to single and married/CU partner filing separate return (MFS is NOT half of MFJ; copied as printed). Civil-union partners must use the corresponding married/CU filing statuses. New Jersey has NO standard deduction — standard_deduction is null because none exists, not because it is income-dependent. NJ instead allows specific deductions on Lines 31-37c (medical expenses over 2% of gross income, alimony, qualified conservation contribution, health enterprise zone, alternative business calculation adjustment, organ/bone marrow donation, up to $10,000 NJBEST 529 contributions, up to $2,500 NJCLASS loan principal and interest, up to $10,000 tuition) and the Line 41 Property Tax Deduction (property taxes paid or 18% of rent, capped at $15,000; $7,500 if married/CU partner filing separately but maintaining the same main home). None of these are modeled. The op applies ONLY the $1,000 Line 6 regular exemption (x exemptions_count) and the $1,500 Line 10/11 dependent exemption (x dependents_count). The result equals Form NJ-1040 Line 43 only when no other exemption (senior, blind/disabled, veteran, college dependent) and no Lines 31-37c or Line 41 deduction applies; otherwise pre-subtract those amounts from the base you supply. NJ exemptions are genuine BASE reductions (Line 13 total -> Line 30, subtracted from gross income before the rates), not credits. Separately, NJ's refundable CREDITS are not modeled: NJ Earned Income Tax Credit (Line 58, 40% of the federal EIC; $260 fixed amount for 2025 age-expansion filers, up from $253 in 2024), the $50 Property Tax Credit (Line 56; $25 if spouses file separately but maintained the same main home), the Child and Dependent Care Credit (Line 64, Worksheet J, 50%/40%/30%/20%/10% of the federal credit by taxable-income band, not eligible over $150,000), the NJ Child Tax Credit (Line 65, up to $1,000 per dependent age 5 or younger, taxable income $80,000 or less), the Wounded Warrior Caregivers Credit (Line 62), and the Credit for Income Taxes Paid to Other Jurisdictions (Line 44, Schedule NJ-COJ). Part-year residents must prorate the Line 13 exemption total on Line 30 by months of NJ residency (15 or more days counts as a month) — NOT modeled; full-year exemption amounts are shipped. No 2025 rate change: the 2025 schedules (top rate 10.75% over $1,000,000) are the statutory schedules in force since tax year 2020, republished unchanged in the final 2025 booklet used for the 2026 filing season; New Jersey had no mid-year retroactive rate legislation for 2025. Return due April 15, 2026. Whole-dollar rounding: the 2025 booklet permits (and the tax table presumes) whole-dollar entries — 'Instead of making dollars-and-cents entries on your return' you may round, dropping amounts under 50 cents and increasing 50 cents or more to the next dollar, which matches this op's irs_round half-up tie behavior.
